notes: Job is almost entirely poetic dialogue (chs. 3-41) framed by thin prose narrative (prologue chs. 1-2, epilogue 42:7-17), so nearly every tier is "person" type rather than "law" — there is no Levitical-style instructional content in this book to theme a law-tier around. Tiers are built around a concrete object/image drawn from each figure's own speech or scene (potsherd, hedge, night-vision/spirit, withering rush, measuring line, new wineskins, whirlwind, horn of eye-paint) rather than abstract theme names. Three deliberate hedges, consistent with accuracy rule 7: (1) Job's wife is not stated by the text to be the mother of Job's second set of children (only that she bore the first set, ch.1) — not asserted as fact. (2) Zophar has no recorded third-cycle speech; some readers associate parts of Job's own ch.26-27 speech with displaced Zophar/friend material, but the text itself attributes all of ch.26-27 to Job (26:1, 27:1), so no third Zophar speech is asserted. (3) Elihu's "kindred of Ram" (32:2) is not identified with any specific Ram named elsewhere (e.g. Ruth 4:19's ancestor of David) — left as an open identification. Naming-collision sweep performed on every character/place name used: Job (flagged per review — collides with Issachar's son "Job" at Gen 46:13, rendered "Jashub" in the Numbers 26:24/1 Chr 7:1 parallels), Eliphaz (collides with Esau's son Eliphaz, Gen 36:4), Elihu (collides with at least three other Elihus: 1 Sam 1:1, 1 Chr 26:7, and the disputed 1 Chr 27:18/Eliab identification), and the shared "Uz"/"Buz" place-names tied to Job's homeland and Elihu's gentilic (both sons of Nahor per Gen 22:20-21). Bildad, Zophar, Jemima, Kezia, and Keren-happuch were checked and no collision was found. No specific real-world identification is asserted for Behemoth (40:15) or Leviathan (ch.41) beyond their KJV names.

genealogyLists.job_first_children: Seven sons and three daughters, all unnamed, born to Job before his trials (Job 1:2); all ten die together when 'there came a great wind from the wilderness' and struck the house where they were feasting (1:18-19).
genealogyLists.job_second_sons: Seven sons born to Job after his restoration (42:13), left unnamed in the text — only the three daughters (Jemima, Kezia, Keren-happuch) are individually named (42:14).
genealogyLists.job_mourners: Job's brethren, sisters, and 'all they that had been of his acquaintance before' who come and eat bread with him after his restoration, each giving him 'a piece of money' and 'an earring of gold' (42:11) — none named individually.
genealogyLists.messengers_of_calamity: Four unnamed messengers arrive in succession reporting the loss of the oxen/asses (1:14-15), sheep (1:16), camels (1:17), and finally Job's children (1:18-19); each closes with 'I only am escaped alone to tell thee.'
genealogyLists.land_of_uz: Job's homeland, 'the land of Uz' (1:1), shares its name with several distinct PERSONS named Uz elsewhere in scripture (Gen 10:23, a son of Aram; Gen 22:21, a son of Nahor/Abraham's brother; Gen 36:28, a Horite/Edomite chief; 1 Chr 1:17,42) — flagged as a name reused across scripture, though in Job 1:1 it functions strictly as a place name, not a personal name.

characters.name: Job
characters.perkNote: Endures the total loss of possessions, children, and health without cursing God (1:20-22, 2:10) and is restored twofold in the epilogue (42:10-17) — the book's central figure.

genealogy.note: Job's own ancestry is not stated in the text; he is introduced only by land of residence (Uz) and character ('perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil,' 1:1). NAMING COLLISION FLAG (explicitly checked per review): the name 'Job' also appears at Genesis 46:13 (KJV) as one of Issachar's sons, 'Tola, and Phuvah, and Job, and Shimron' — a completely different individual from the protagonist of this book. That same son is rendered 'Jashub' in the parallel genealogical lists at Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1, confirming the Genesis 46:13 spelling is a distinct name-form for a distinct person, not this Job.
children: Seven unnamed sons and three unnamed daughters, first set, all deceased (1:2, 18-19)
Seven unnamed sons, second set, born after restoration (42:13)

verses.note: Introduced as a blameless, wealthy man of Uz — 'the greatest of all the men of the east.'
Response to the first calamities: 'the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD... In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.'
Struck with sore boils; rebukes his wife's counsel to curse God — 'shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?'
Job's opening lament, cursing the day of his birth, breaking the seven days of silence.
Job's closing self-defense and oath of innocence before the whirlwind speeches.
Final response to the LORD: 'now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.'
Lives 140 years after his restoration, sees four generations, and 'died, being old and full of days.'

funFacts: Named alongside Noah and Daniel as an exemplar of righteousness in Ezekiel 14:14,20 — a real cross-book reference, not this book's own claim.
Cited by name in the New Testament for his patience: 'Ye have heard of the patience of Job' (James 5:11).
His possessions exactly double after restoration: 7,000 sheep to 14,000, 3,000 camels to 6,000, 500 yoke of oxen to 1,000, 500 she asses to 1,000 (1:3 vs 42:12).

characters.name: Job's wife (unnamed)
characters.perkNote: Her one recorded scene is oppositional, not supportive — she urges Job to 'curse God, and die' (2:9), prompting his rebuke — so she is flavored as opposing/incidental to Job's arc despite being family, per the methodology's action-based (not relation-based) flavor rule.

genealogy.note: Never named in the book. The text does not explicitly state whether she is also the mother of Job's second set of restored children (42:13-14) — only that she bore the first set (implied by 1:2-19); this is not asserted as fact here.
children: Same first set of children as Job (1:2); relation to the second, restored set is not explicitly stated by the text

verses.note: 'Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die' — Job rebukes her as speaking 'as one of the foolish women speaketh.'
Job later laments, 'My breath is strange to my wife, though I intreated for the children's sake of mine own body' — the only other likely reference to her in the book.

funFacts: Never given a name in the KJV text of Job.

characters.name: Satan
characters.perkNote: Instigates both stages of the wager permitted by God (1:9-12, 2:4-6) — the narrative engine behind Job's affliction.

genealogy.note: Not a human figure — one of 'the sons of God' who present themselves before the LORD (1:6, 2:1); no human ancestry is stated or applicable. The same name/title 'Satan' appears elsewhere in the KJV for what is generally understood to be the same accusing figure (1 Chronicles 21:1; Zechariah 3:1-2) — noted here as the same name reused, not as a different person requiring a collision flag.

verses.note: Appears among 'the sons of God' before the LORD; asks 'Doth Job fear God for nought?'
'Hast not thou made an hedge about him...?' — granted power over Job's possessions and children, but not his person.
Second appearance; 'Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life' — granted power to strike Job's body, but 'save his life.'
'Smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown.'

funFacts: Never again appears or is referenced after chapter 2 — absent from the epilogue entirely.

characters.name: Eliphaz the Temanite
characters.perkNote: First and most frequent of the three friends to speak (chs. 4-5, 15, 22); the only one directly addressed by name in God's rebuke (42:7).

genealogy.note: No ancestry given in Job beyond the gentilic 'the Temanite' (from Teman). NAMING COLLISION FLAG: 'Eliphaz' is also the name of Esau's firstborn son by Adah, ancestor of the Edomites/Amalekites (Genesis 36:4,10-12,15-16; 1 Chronicles 1:35-36) — a distinct individual from Eliphaz the Temanite here. Notably, that OTHER Eliphaz's own son Teman (Genesis 36:11) is the namesake of this Eliphaz's home region — a geographically suggestive echo, but Job's text never states any genealogical link between the two Eliphazes, so none is asserted.

verses.note: First speech, first cycle: 'Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent?'
Recounts a night vision: 'a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up.'
Second speech, sharper in tone, accuses Job of arrogance against God.
Third speech, levels specific (unproven) accusations of sin against Job.

Named directly in the LORD's rebuke ('my wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends') and commanded, with Bildad and Zophar, to offer seven bullocks and seven rams while Job prays for them.

funFacts: Given three separate speeches (chs. 4-5, 15, 22) — more than any other friend.

characters.name: Bildad the Shuhite
characters.perkNote: Argues from the accumulated wisdom of 'the former age' (8:8-10) across three speeches (chs. 8, 18, 25).

genealogy.note: No ancestry given beyond the gentilic 'the Shuhite' (possibly from Shuah, a son of Abraham by Keturah, Genesis 25:2 — a place/name link the text of Job itself never confirms, so not asserted as fact). Checked for naming collisions: no other person named 'Bildad' is found elsewhere in scripture.

verses.note: First speech: appeals to 'the former age'; 'Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?'
Second speech, on the fate and fear of the wicked.
Third speech — markedly short, only six verses, compared to his first two.
Named among the three friends who obey the LORD's command to offer sacrifice and receive Job's intercession.

funFacts: His third-cycle speech (ch. 25) is the shortest of any friend's speech in the book — six verses.

characters.name: Zophar the Naamathite
characters.perkNote: Sharpest and most direct of the three friends across his two recorded speeches (chs. 11, 20).

genealogy.note: No ancestry given beyond the gentilic 'the Naamathite' (from a place called Naamah, distinct from persons elsewhere named Naamah — e.g. Genesis 4:22, Lamech's daughter; 1 Kings 14:21, Solomon's Ammonite wife — and distinct from Naaman the Syrian; noted as a name-family worth flagging even though 'Naamathite' itself does not collide directly with those personal names). Checked for direct collisions on 'Zophar': none found elsewhere in scripture.

verses.note: First speech: 'Canst thou by searching find out God?... The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.'
Second speech, on the brief triumph and downfall of the wicked.
Named among the three friends who obey the LORD's command to offer sacrifice and receive Job's intercession.

funFacts: Unlike Eliphaz and Bildad, no third-cycle speech is recorded for Zophar in the text. Chapters 26-27 (which some readers associate with retribution-theology content similar to the friends' arguments) are explicitly attributed to Job himself speaking (26:1, 27:1), so a 'missing' or displaced Zophar speech is not asserted as fact here — only the observed gap in the text.

characters.name: Elihu the Buzite
characters.perkNote: Speaks last among the human interlocutors (chs. 32-37), claiming fresh insight because of his youth (32:6-7) — his speech leads directly into the whirlwind.

genealogy.note: The only one of the four human interlocutors given an explicit genealogy in the text: 'Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram' (32:2) — the specific identity of this 'kindred of Ram' is not further specified and is not equated here with any other Ram named elsewhere (e.g. the ancestor of David in Ruth 4:19), a genuinely open identification. NAMING COLLISION FLAG: 'Elihu' is reused for at least three other distinct persons in scripture — an ancestor of Samuel, an Ephrathite (1 Samuel 1:1); a Korahite Levite gatekeeper's kinsman (1 Chronicles 26:7); and 'Elihu, one of the brethren of David,' named ruler over Judah (1 Chronicles 27:18), sometimes thought to be another name for Eliab, David's oldest brother (cf. 1 Samuel 16:6, 17:13) — an identification the text does not make explicit, so treated as disputed, not fact. None of these are the Elihu of this book.

verses.note: Introduced; his anger is kindled against Job for justifying himself rather than God, and against the three friends for condemning Job without answering him.
Explains his silence until now: 'I am young, and ye are very old... Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom.'
'I am full of matter, the spirit within me constraineth me. Behold, my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles.'
Argues God speaks to men through dreams and visions of the night to turn them from their purpose.
'Hearken unto this, O Job: stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God' — closing appeal, immediately preceding the LORD's own speech.

funFacts: The only human speaker given a full genealogy in the text (32:2).

His gentilic 'Buzite' shares a namesake with Buz, a son of Nahor (Abraham's brother) paired with his brother Uz in Genesis 22:20-21 — the same 'Uz' name as Job's own homeland (Job 1:1). The text of Job does not claim either man is a literal descendant of these specific Genesis figures; this is noted only as a textual echo, not an asserted genealogy.
Never mentioned again after chapter 37, and not named among the friends addressed in the LORD's rebuke (42:7-9) — the text is silent on why, so no explanation is asserted here.

characters.name: The LORD
characters.perkNote: Speaks directly to Job out of the whirlwind across two speeches (38:1, 40:6) — the book's climactic, pivotal event, per its own emphasis on creation and the limits of human understanding rather than a direct explanation of Job's suffering.

genealogy.note: Not applicable — the LORD is not a created being with human ancestry; appears and speaks directly in the narrative (38:1) rather than being described genealogically.

verses.note: 'Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind... Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?' — opens the first speech.
Continues, questioning Job about wild animals: the lion, raven, wild goat, wild ass, the unicorn (KJV), the ostrich, the horse, the hawk, and the eagle.
First pause: 'Shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him?'
Second speech begins by describing Behemoth, 'which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox' — no specific real-world animal is identified by the text itself.
Describes Leviathan: 'Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?' — likewise not identified with any specific real-world creature by the text.
After Job's response, the LORD rebukes the three friends by name (Eliphaz first) and instructs them to offer sacrifice through Job's intercession.

funFacts: Answers entirely through rhetorical questions across both speeches, never directly stating why Job suffered — the book's climax is a confrontation with divine power and order, not an explanation.

characters.name: Jemima
characters.perkNote: Named first of Job's three restored daughters, granted an inheritance alongside her seven brothers (42:15) — an explicitly unusual arrangement for the custom of the time.

genealogy.note: Mother not named in the text (Job's wife is never named in the book). Named first among the three daughters born after Job's restoration (42:14); the text gives no differentiated action between the three sisters beyond birth order and their shared, unusual inheritance (42:15). Checked for naming collisions: no other person named 'Jemima' is found elsewhere in scripture.

verses.note: 'He had also seven sons and three daughters. And he called the name of the first, Jemima.'
'In all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job: and their father gave them inheritance among their brethren.'

funFacts: Job's grant of inheritance to his daughters alongside seven living sons runs counter to the ordinary practice reflected in Numbers 27:8, where daughters inherit only in the absence of sons — the text itself flags this as remarkable.

characters.name: Kezia
characters.perkNote: A sister sharing equally in Job's restored household and its unusual inheritance — boosts Jemima's tier as a direct family supporter.

genealogy.note: Second of the three daughters named in 42:14; the text does not differentiate her individual actions from her sisters beyond the shared inheritance note in 42:15. Checked for naming collisions: no other person named 'Kezia' is found elsewhere in scripture.

verses.note: Named second among Job's three post-restoration daughters.

funFacts: Her name means 'cassia,' a fragrant spice — like her sisters' names, evocative rather than narratively differentiating.

characters.name: Keren-happuch
characters.perkNote: A sister sharing equally in Job's restored household and its unusual inheritance — boosts Jemima's tier as a direct family supporter.

genealogy.note: Third and last of the three daughters named in 42:14; the text does not differentiate her individual actions from her sisters beyond the shared inheritance note in 42:15. Checked for naming collisions: no other person named 'Keren-happuch' is found elsewhere in scripture.

verses.note: Named third and last among Job's three post-restoration daughters; her name ('horn of eye-paint,' i.e. a cosmetic-pigment container) is this tier's namesake.

funFacts: Her name references a horn-shaped container for cosmetic eye-paint (antimony), a real object of the period.
